clips.send: Angel Island, San Francisco Bay. Open 1910–1940. Many arrivals came from China and Japan. Because of the Chinese Exclusion Act (《排华法案》, 1882), Chinese immigrants were often held for weeks or months and questioned closely. Detainees carved poems in Chinese into the wooden walls — you can still read them today. The law was not repealed until 1943, when China was a US ally in World War II.

clips.send: Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. 17 December 1903. Orville and Wilbur Wright, bicycle makers from Dayton, Ohio, chose the windy sand dunes at Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk. clips.send: Ellis Island, New York Harbor. Open 1892–1954. Before 1892, New York’s immigrants came through Castle Garden (1855–1890) at the tip of Manhattan. clips.send: Detroit, Michigan. Model T 1908, moving assembly line 1913. Henry Ford’s Model T (1908) was built to be simple, tough and cheap. In 1913 Ford’s Highland Park plant added a moving assembly line (流水线 liúshuǐxiàn): building a chassis dropped from about 12½ hours to about 1½ hours. The price fell from $850 (1908) to under $400 by 1916 — ordinary families could buy a car.

clips.send: The first transcontinental railroad. Golden spike: 10 May 1869. Union Pacific built west from Omaha; Central Pacific built east from Sacramento. They met at Promontory Summit, Utah. A coast-to-coast trip shrank from months to about a week.

clips.send: Tuskegee Institute, Alabama. Carver arrives 1896. Born enslaved in Missouri, Carver became a scientist and teacher at Tuskegee. Growing only cotton wore out Southern soil. He taught farmers crop rotation (轮作) with peanuts and sweet potatoes, which put nitrogen back in the soil. He found hundreds of uses for peanuts, sweet potatoes and other crops to give farmers new markets.

clips.send: Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Steel city from 1875. Andrew Carnegie opened his Edgar Thomson Steel Works near Pittsburgh in 1875, using the Bessemer process (贝塞麦炼钢法) to make cheap steel. Coal from nearby hills and three rivers for shipping made it the perfect spot. Steel went into rails, bridges and skyscrapers. Thousands of immigrants from Eastern Europe worked in the mills.

clips.send: The Chisholm Trail. Used about 1867–1884. After the Civil War, a longhorn steer worth about $4 in Texas could sell for around $40 in the North — a price incentive (价格刺激) that drove the trail. Cowboys drove herds of a few thousand cattle about 10–12 miles a day for weeks, to railheads like Abilene, Kansas. Millions of cattle went up the trails. Many cowboys were Black or Mexican American. Barbed wire and new rail lines into Texas ended the long drives by the late 1880s.

clips.send: 亚拉巴马州塔斯基吉学院。1896年卡弗来到这里。卡弗生于密苏里州的奴隶家庭，后来成为塔斯基吉学院的科学家和教师。只种棉花让南方土地变得贫瘠。他教农民用花生和红薯轮作（crop rotation），让土壤恢复氮肥。他为花生、红薯等作物找到了数百种用途，帮农民打开新市场。

clips.send: 第一条横贯大陆铁路。1869年5月10日钉下“金道钉”。联合太平洋铁路从奥马哈向西修，中央太平洋铁路从萨克拉门托向东修，两路在犹他州海角点（Promontory Summit）会合。中央太平洋铁路雇用了成千上万名华工，高峰时占其工人的大多数。他们在内华达山脉的花岗岩中开凿隧道。横穿大陆的时间从几个月缩短到大约一周。

clips.send: 奇泽姆小道（Chisholm Trail）。约1867—1884年使用。南北战争后，一头长角牛在得克萨斯约值4美元，在北方能卖到约40美元——这种价格刺激（price incentive）推动了长途赶牛。牛仔赶着几千头牛，每天走10—12英里，连走几个星期，到达堪萨斯州阿比林等铁路小镇。数以百万计的牛经这些小道北上。许多牛仔是黑人或墨西哥裔。到19世纪80年代后期，带刺铁丝网和通到得克萨斯的新铁路让长途赶牛走向结束。
